name: Poch (Pochen)
description: Poch (or Pochen) is an ancient German family game documented as far back as 1441. It is widely recognized as one of the primary ancestors of modern Poker, particularly for its 'Pochen' (vying or betting) phase. Played with a specialized board (Pochbrett), it combines elements of luck, betting, and strategic card-shedding. It is a 'Three-in-One' game where a single deal is used to play three distinct sub-games, rewarded by different portions of a central pot.
deck: 32-card German or Piquet deck (7s to Aces)

history.origins: One of the oldest recorded card games in European history. The name 'Pochen' means 'to brag' or 'to knock' (on the table to indicate a bet), which evolved into the word 'Poker'.
timeline: 1441: First historical mention in Strasbourg, Germany.
1600s: Becomes a staple in German and French courts as 'Poque'.
1800s: Influences the developement of English 'Brag' and American 'Poker'.
Present: Still played in traditional German social clubs and as a historical folk game.
history.cultural: Traditional versions use a wooden board with nine carved bowls to hold tokens, making it as much a 'Board Game' as a card game.
history.evolution: The transition to the United States via French 'Poque' players in New Orleans is the missing link that led to the creation of the 5-card Poker game known today.

setup.dealing: Dealer deals clockwise one card at a time until one card remains; that card is turned face up to set the pay suit (trump). In the 5-cards-each variant, five cards per player then one card turned for trump. Before each deal every player antes one chip to each of the nine pools.
setup.equipment: Poch board (Pochbrett) with nine pools for stakes: Ace, King, Queen, Jack, Ten, Marriage, Sequence (7-8-9), Pochen (Joker), and centre pot (Pinke).

rules.objective: Win chips from the Poch-board by holding specific cards, winning the bet, and being the first to shed all cards.
rules.gameplay: Three stages per deal. Stage 1 (sweepstakes): players with Ace, King, Queen, Jack or Ten of the pay suit collect from those pools; King+Queen of pay suit wins Marriage; 7-8-9 of pay suit wins Sequence. Stage 2 (Pochen): players bet on best set (four of a kind beats three of a kind beats pair); pass, bet, match or raise, or fold; best set wins Pochen pool and all stakes; winner (or left of dealer if all pass) leads Stage 3. Stage 3 (shedding): play any card; whoever has next higher in same suit plays; sequence continues until no one can play; last to play starts a new sequence; first out of cards wins centre pot plus one chip per card from each opponent.
keyRules: Before each deal every player puts one chip in each of the nine board pools.
Pay suit (trump) is the suit of the turned card; it breaks ties in Pochen (pair with pay-suit card beats same-rank pair).
In Pochen only pairs, triples and fours of a kind count; higher set beats lower; you may pass or drop out and forfeit stakes already placed.
In the shedding stage you must play the next higher card in the same suit when you have it; the player who played the last card of a sequence leads the next.

strategy.basic: Conserve your high cards for Phase 3! While you might want to use your Aces to win a bet in Phase 2, an Ace is a 'Stop' card in Phase 3. If you hold an Ace, you have the power to stop an opponent's sequence and start your own, which is the fastest way to win the shedding round. Don't go 'All-In' during the Pochen phase unless you have at least 3-of-a-kind; the competition for the central pot is fierce.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Pinke' Bluff: Because you don't always have to show your hand if everyone else folds, use the Pochen phase to bluff as if you have a high set. If you win that pot, you get the initiative to lead in the shedding phase. Choice of the lead card in Phase 3 is 50% of the game; lead a suit you are 'Long' in to control the board.
strategy.advanced: Marriage Management: If you hold the King of Trump but not the Queen, watch the board. If no one claims the 'Marriage' bowl in Phase 1, it stays there and grows. In the next round, if you hold the Queen, you can aggressively bid to win the right to name trump (in some variants) or just play defensively to ensure you capture that overflowing bowl later.
tips: Always follow the sequence in Phase 3! If you forget your card and someone else plays it, you lose your turn.
If you have a 4-of-a-kind, you are almost guaranteed the Phase 2 pot. Don't be afraid to raise to the maximum.

scoring.winCondition: Game continues until a player cannot ante (lacks nine chips for the next deal). Winner is the player with the most chips; first to shed all cards in a deal wins the centre pot and one chip per card from each opponent for that deal.
